Hi Zane (and the statnet user group),
I've been corresponding with Martina Morris and I've been able to fix my
data, so the ergm works even with my missing attribute data (on average
20%).

There was something about the formatting of my missing data (imported from
STATA) that seemed to impact the statnet refusing to define my attribute
data. Hopefully my solution will help others who have had issues with
missing attribute data.  I did not need to impute!

Here's the code that I used
#make sure your variables are factored if they are factor variables
#I am using a dataset called JeffFactor where my categorical variables are
defined as factor variables in R
#Cutting down the number of variables used in the data
myvars <- c("biof", hispanic","race", "grade")
JeffDem <- JeffFactor[myvars]
attach(JeffDem)
#ensure missing has appropriate prefix
JeffDem$biof <- Recode(JeffDem$biof, 'NA=NA', as.factor.result=FALSE)
JeffDem$race <- Recode(JeffDem$race, 'NA=NA', as.factor.result=FALSE)
#mark as missing in R
JeffDem$biof[NA] <-NA
JeffDem$race <- Recode(JeffDem$race, 'NA=NA', as.factor.result=FALSE)
#define your adjacency matrix
relations <-net
relations %v% "race" <- JeffDem$race
relations %v% "gender" <-JeffDem$biof
#fit ergm
jmodel.01 <- ergm(relations~edges+nodematch('race', diff=T))

-Karen Ertrachter

On Wed, Jan 29, 2014 at 8:58 PM, Carter T. Butts <buttsc@uci.edu> wrote:
> Hi, Michal. The current version of ergm() will, when given a network with
> missing edges, find the observed-data MLE under the assumption that the
> observed data is ignorably sampled from the graph being modeled. H+G discuss
> the conditions under which that is a reasonable assumption...but where it
> is, ergm() should work out of the box.
>
> An alternative approach (closer to what is in the tutorial you mention) is
> to obtain an approximate MLE by (1) using design-based estimation to obtain
> (approximate) sufficient statistics, and (2) fitting to those target stats
> (using the functionality currently in ERGM). Note that to do this in a valid
> manner, the graph used for simulation in ERGM must be of the same size as
> the graph from which your data was sampled -- this means that the method
> does not scale so well if one has a really large system (e.g., an OSN). One
> advantage of this approach is that it makes it easier to relax the
> assumption that the seed nodes for the link-trace were drawn from a
> probability sample (by using Markov chain-based sampling methods - see,
> e.g., Gjoka et al., IEEE JSAC, 2011). (Of course, that only helps you if you
> are in a position to choose your data collection design!) If your
> design-based estimators are consistent, then the associated approximate MLE
> should be consistent as well, but your measures of standard error will in
> general be underestimated (because they neglect the sampling variability in
> your estimates of the sufficient statistics). My impression is that Pavel is
> currently working on this (or, if not, a closely related problem!).
>
> Mark or others may want to chime in on this, but that should at least give
> you the basic rundown....
>
> -Carter
>

Hi folks,
I don't know if questions about this would be better posted elsewhere, but this seemed the logical list to me. I am having a minor issue getting colors to plot in the manner i'd expect within ndtv. I am specifying node color as a TEA based on vertex attributes on the network objects. Instead of using those values as the color vector, it appears to be using a "unique sort" on values and assigning colors to those sequentially. Is there a way to get it to do the former instead?
 
In other words (trivial example, code below), suppose the values in slice 1 of the color variable are 1, 2, 3, while in slice 2 they are 1, 2, 4. What I would expect is that slice 1 would have 3 colors, slice 2 would also have 3, but only 2 of them would be the same (i.e., those with label 4 in slice 2 should NOT be the same as those with label 3 in slice 1). However, what i'm getting is that each slice is using the same 3-color palette. Plotting the three initial network objects w/plot.network gives the result I was anticipating. Am i missing something obvious?

thanks!
jimi

Trivial example code:
t1 <- network.initialize(3)
add.edge(t1,1,2) 
add.edge(t1,2,3)
t1 <- set.vertex.attribute(t1, "col", c(1:3))
t2 <- t1
t2 <- set.vertex.attribute(t2, "col", c(1,2,4))
t3 <- t2
ex <- networkDynamic(network.list=list(t1, t2, t3), vertex.pid="vertex.names", create.TEAs=T)
compute.animation(ex, slice.par=list(start=1,end=3,interval=1, aggregate.dur=1,rule='all'))
render.animation(ex, vertex.col="col")

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jimi, great to see you are trying out the ndtv package!

On 02/04/2014 11:09 AM, jimi adams wrote:
> Hi folks,
> I don't know if questions about this would be better posted elsewhere, but this seemed the logical list to me.

This is definitely the right place to ask ndtv questions :-)

I am having a minor issue getting colors to plot in the manner i'd 
expect within ndtv. I am specifying node color as a TEA based on vertex 
attributes on the network objects. Instead of using those values as the 
color vector, it appears to be using a "unique sort" on values and 
assigning colors to those sequentially. Is there a way to get it to do 
the former instead?
>
> In other words (trivial example, code below), suppose the values in slice 1 of the color variable are 1, 2, 3, while in slice 2 they are 1, 2, 4. What I would expect is that slice 1 would have 3 colors, slice 2 would also have 3, but only 2 of them would be the same (i.e., those with label 4 in slice 2 should NOT be the same as those with label 3 in slice 1). However, what i'm getting is that each slice is using the same 3-color palette. Plotting the three initial network objects w/plot.network gives the result I was anticipating. Am i missing something obvious?

I think the issue is that you are plotting the wrong time range for the 
example network. I'll expand on your example below.

>
> thanks!
> jimi
>
> Trivial example code:
> t1 <- network.initialize(3)
> add.edge(t1,1,2)
> add.edge(t1,2,3)
> t1 <- set.vertex.attribute(t1, "col", c(1:3))
> t2 <- t1
> t2 <- set.vertex.attribute(t2, "col", c(1,2,4))
> t3 <- t2
> ex <- networkDynamic(network.list=list(t1, t2, t3), vertex.pid="vertex.names", create.TEAs=T)
> compute.animation(ex, slice.par=list(start=1,end=3,interval=1, aggregate.dur=1,rule='all'))
> render.animation(ex, vertex.col="col")

Note that when you called networkDynamic(), it reported that it was 
making some default assumptions:

"Neither start or onsets specified, assuming start=0
Onsets and termini not specified, assuming each network in network.list 
should have a discrete spell of length 1"

This may be confusing, but what it means is that the first network on 
the list will be start at 0 and extend until 1, the 2nd will start at 1 
and extend until 2, etc.

For this example you computed a movie for the range 1 to 3, so you were 
only viewing the values from the t2 network onward

If I directly query the values of the attributes at each time I see

 > get.vertex.attribute.active(ex,'col',at=0)
[1] 1 2 3
 > get.vertex.attribute.active(ex,'col',at=1)
[1] 1 2 4
 > get.vertex.attribute.active(ex,'col',at=2)
[1] 1 2 4

I re-ran the movie, shifting slice.par one unit earlier:

compute.animation(ex,slice.par=list(start=0,end=2,interval=1,aggregate.dur=1,rule='all'))
render.animation(ex, vertex.col="col")

I see the color of vertex '3' change from green to blue, which seems 
like what you were expecting, right?

Alternatively, if you want the "ex" network to actually start at time 1 
instead of 0, you can explicitly tell the networkDynamic() converter 
function when the first start time should be using the "start" parameter:

ex <- networkDynamic(network.list=list(t1, t2, 
t3),vertex.pid="vertex.names", create.TEAs=T,start=1)

or even give it the onset and terminus of each panel if they have 
different durations or you want to use different time units...

ex <- networkDynamic(network.list=list(t1, t2, t3), 
vertex.pid="vertex.names", create.TEAs=T,onsets=1:3,termini=2:4)


Please let me know if this resolves the issue.

best,
  -skye

conference workshop on plotting dynamic networks with the ndtv package 
on Tueseday Feb 18. I think there are still a few slots left...

Karen,

One last point -- it's not a good idea to use nodematch terms without also 
using the associated nodefactor.  nodematch is a bit like an interaction 
effect in a glm, the interaction of attr(node 1) x attr(node 2).  As in 
most modeling, if you include an interaction of two variables, you 
probably want to include the main effects for them also.

So, bottom line for this model, I would suggest:

1. use a nodefactor term for every attribute you're also nodematching on

2. if you want to exclude the intercept, make sure you use 
nodefactor('attrname', base=0) (thanks to Steve for reminding me of this)

3. see if this works before getting fancy with ergm controls of various 
kinds

best,
Martina

Rose,

When you say "control a multiple 2-path model", it's not clear exactly 
what you mean.

At this point the ergm term "gwesp", when used on a directed network, 
counts one possible configuration:  only partners on a directed two-path 
connecting the nodes in the dyad.

You might try looking at the terms "balance", "intransitive", 
"transitive", "transitiveties", "triadcensus", and "triangle"
to see if any of these do what you want.

Note that ergm is an open source package, and it is possible to code your 
own terms (see the  ergm.userterms package and paper for details).

Martina

You should adjust for network size using the offset described in Pavel

messages.body_plain:
Ji Youn,

First, how large is your network (#nodes #edges)?  You have quite a few 
terms in this model, so your net should be large enough to accomodate 
them.

Second, you might try starting with a simple model, and then work up 
adding terms, to see when the problem emerges.  I'd suggest starting with 
the dyad independent terms (adding one at a time), and once all of these 
have been added, then add the dyad dependent terms one at a time (first 
the degree terms, then the esps).

If you set the decay term to 0, it counts only the first occurence of the 
statistic (rather than declining marginal returns on each additional 
occurrence).  So it may be worth starting with this.

You should also try using the summary command on the model terms to see 
what the distributions look like in the data.

hth,
Martina

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Working with multiplex networks
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jacques,
  Although the network data structure facilitates multiplex ties, there 
is very little network or statnet functionality that is directly aware 
of them.   I'm including some example operations below, including 
tracking tie types with an attached attribute.  We should probably have 
some more specific multiplex functions in the network package 
(suggestions welcome).

best,
  -skye


## some toy example operations on a multiplex network ##

multi<-network.initialize(5,multiple=TRUE)

is.multiplex(multi)

# add parallel edges between v1 and v2
# also add an attribute names 'type' to each tie
multi<-add.edges(multi,tail=c(1,1,1,1),head=c(2,2,3,4),names.eval='type',vals.eval=c("A","B","A","B"))

# get ids of edges linking v1 and v2
get.edgeIDs(multi,v=1,alter=2)


# plot the types in different colors with some transparency to show overlap
plot(multi,edge.col=ifelse(multi%e%'type'=='A','#00FF0055','#0000FF55'),edge.lwd=10)

# get the ids of all edges with type B
which(get.edge.attribute(multi,'type')=='B')

# create a new network with only type B edges

multiB<-multi
multiB<-delete.edges(multiB,eid=which(get.edge.attribute(multi,'type')!='B'))
multiB%e%'type'
